title: AI Labs Want Someone to Stop Them

illustration.alt: Dario Amodei holds an AI safety plan outside a meeting room for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, while antitrust tape blocks the doorway and a huge frontier-AI computer races onward.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Frontier AI labs spend billions on computing to keep producing premium models. A coordinated slowdown could lower their costs and extend premium pricing, but an agreement among competitors to limit development could violate antitrust law.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: The AI labs may want to cooperate to prevent rogue AI from killing everyone, yet antitrust law designed to protect society from colluding companies might prevent that cooperation.

preschool.title: The Race That Nobody Could Pause
preschool.lesson: If frontier AI companies jointly slow development, they could reduce computing costs and keep charging premium prices longer, but that coordination may count as an illegal agreement among competitors to limit output.
paragraphs:
Anthropic may go public; its pitch could declare
a market above $30 trillion waiting out there.
SpaceX estimated $28.5 trillion; Anthropic’s claim
would be finance’s biggest market target by name.

The sunny case: AI does one quarter of work everywhere,
and Anthropic captures it all as its share.
The stormy case Dario Amodei fears is more grim:
rogue AI could end everyone—not merely the firm.

So Dario urged companies to “pace” the frontier race,
with shared safety limits to keep danger in its place.
He asked for government help or an antitrust waiver,
so labs could coordinate without unlawful behavior.

If all pause together, compute bills may fall,
while premium frontier prices last longer for all.
But competitors agreeing to limit what they make
can look like a cartel—and the law hits the brake.

The strangest snag waits at the conference-room door:
the labs say their race could bring danger galore.
Yet rules built to stop rivals from rigging the game
might bar them from joining to slow the AI train.

What happened? Dario Amodei proposed that frontier AI companies coordinate on safety standards and limits, with government mediation or antitrust waivers. Such coordination could reduce costly model development and preserve high prices, but it might also be treated as an illegal agreement among competitors to restrict output.

illustration.alt: SpaceX insiders stand by an opened lockup gate while holding their shares, as Nasdaq 100 index-fund buyers approach from a later calendar page.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: When IPO lockups expire, more shares become freely tradable, increasing float; a float-adjusted index may recognize the increase only during a later rebalancing, when index funds must buy shares to match the higher weight.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: The same lockup expiration creates both potential sellers and eventual index-fund buyers, but they arrive weeks apart instead of trading neatly with each other.

preschool.title: The Buyers Who Came Late
preschool.lesson: A lockup expiration can increase a stock’s tradable float immediately, while index funds may not buy the added weight until a later index rebalancing.
paragraphs:
When SpaceX offered stock to all,
most shares stayed locked behind a wall.
An IPO makes shares public; a lock
makes insiders wait before selling their stock.

The shares free to trade are known as “float.”
Index weights take that amount into note.
When locked shares open for buying and sale,
the float grows bigger on the index’s scale.

The first SpaceX lockup ended in August;
a second expired one week later, as promised.
Some feared that a flood of shares would appear—
but insiders mostly held, and no selloff came near.

Yet Nasdaq did not change the weight that same day.
Its scheduled adjustment was farther away.
Isabelle Lee reported the later forecast:
SpaceX’s index share would rise quite fast—

from roughly 1.28% of the Nasdaq 100 mix
to about 2.82% when Nasdaq made the fix.
Passive funds copy the index just so;
with SpaceX weighted higher, their buying must grow.

That could mean billions in purchases—but late!
The possible sellers and buyers missed their date.
One lockup caused both sides of the affair,
yet the market’s two calendars would not pair.

Hedge funds could buy and hold every share,
then sell to index funds when they finally got there.
But warehousing stock brings risk, cost, and strain.
Why not let both crowds meet on the same day’s train?

What happened? SpaceX’s lockup expirations increased the shares available to trade, but the Nasdaq 100 was expected to recognize that larger float only at a later rebalancing, raising SpaceX’s projected weight from about 1.28% to about 2.82%. That delay separated possible insider selling from billions of dollars of expected passive-fund buying.

illustration.alt: Rick Phillips and Carlos Dias Jr. examine newly corrected insurance files showing more than $20 billion in affiliated loans, while Mark Walter stands beside TWG Global holdings and a Los Angeles Lakers stake-sale document.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Annuity customers paid upfront for fixed returns, while the insurers invested substantial funds in loans to affiliated businesses; more than $20 billion of those loans were not correctly labeled as affiliated transactions until after subpoenas.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: TWG Global argued that nobody had been harmed because the loans and annuities had not defaulted—and customers supposedly never read the disclosures—only for an annuity customer and a financial adviser to notice and become worried.

preschool.title: The Annuities Somebody Read
preschool.lesson: Insurers must correctly disclose loans to affiliated businesses so regulators, rating agencies, advisers, and annuity customers can judge the risks behind promised payments.
paragraphs:
Mark Walter’s TWG Global had holdings galore:
Big sports-team stakes and insurance firms in its store.
Delaware Life and Clear Spring Life and Annuity
sold contracts designed to provide payment security.

Customers paid money up front for returns that stayed fixed,
while insurers chose where those funds would be mixed.
More than $20 billion went out as loans
to businesses linked to the same owner’s zones.

Those loans should have carried an “affiliated” name,
but the insurers’ disclosures did not say the same.
After subpoenas arrived, the true labels appeared;
prosecutors asked questions, and regulators peered.

TWG Global said, “There is no victim here.”
The loans had not failed; payments still did appear.
And because private investments aren’t traded each day,
no falling market price flashed trouble their way.

Besides, annuity buyers don’t read every sheet—
so who would complain if the payments stayed neat?
But Rick Phillips read news that made confidence fall:
Walter planned to sell his controlling stake in the Los Angeles Lakers after all.

Adviser Carlos Dias Jr. had trusted strong ratings,
healthy disclosures, and calm calculations.
Then AM Best considered a possible downgrade;
the hidden affiliate totals left both men afraid.

So customers may skip many footnotes—quite true.
But Rick and Carlos showed that somebody reads a few.
No missed payment was needed to make concern start:
wrong labels can hide a risk’s most important part.

What happened? Clear Spring Life and Annuity and Delaware Life disclosed more than $20 billion of loans that should have been labeled as transactions with affiliated businesses but were not. The annuities kept paying, yet the corrected disclosures and possible rating downgrade worried customer Rick Phillips and adviser Carlos Dias Jr.

illustration.alt: Alex Richardson watches landlords deliver tenant-improvement checks to newly opening Guidepost schools while an older location displays a $50,000 monthly loss bill.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Landlords provided large upfront tenant-improvement advances for new Guidepost schools; rapid expansion generated fresh cash, but ongoing school losses and later obligations made the model unsustainable when expansion stopped.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: A Montessori preschool chain allegedly resembled a Ponzi scheme because opening more schools supplied cash needed while schools lost money—and after bankruptcy, some Montessori programs were replaced with artificial intelligence, which was presented as another supposedly promising model.

preschool.title: The Schools That Had to Keep Opening
preschool.lesson: Higher Ground received upfront landlord advances when opening Guidepost schools, but continuing losses and later obligations made expansion unsustainable once new openings—and their fresh cash—stopped.
paragraphs:
Guidepost schools were expensive to run,
but opening each new one brought money in.
Landlords advanced cash to improve every place,
so expanding supplied Higher Ground with financial grace.

That cash became “float”—money held for a spell,
though bills and repayments would come due as well.
Alex Richardson, a teacher there early,
called it a “Montessori Ponzi” quite clearly.

New schools kept opening at remarkable speed:
thirty-three in 2020, then twenty-one more indeed.
Yet some Guidepost locations, month after month,
were losing $50,000—not merely a bunch.

Kevin McDonald advanced $1 million, he said,
for a Guidepost in Ellisville to get up and spread.
He estimated not even one-third reached that school,
and believed other openings had swallowed the pool.

Co-founder Ray Girn firmly denied wrongdoing,
calling the model misunderstood, not negligent doing.
But losses reached $154.6 million in all,
and without further growth, the company took a fall.

Claire Suddath reported one final surprise:
some California schools changed after their sale and demise.
Their Montessori curriculum was swept away,
to be replaced by artificial intelligence—also promising, they’d say.

What happened? Higher Ground often received landlord advances when it opened Guidepost schools, providing fresh cash while existing schools lost money and obligations accumulated. After rapid expansion stopped, the company collapsed into bankruptcy; the quoted claims about diverted funds were allegations disputed by Ray Girn.

illustration.alt: An AI researcher holds a huge compensation contract beside a retirement door while Anastasia Koroleva interviews a founder with a $500 million sale document and Sherry Walling holds Exit Strategy.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: AI firms must offer compensation high enough to compete for top researchers, but that compensation can let employees retire immediately; likewise, a large company sale creates an exit that removes a founder’s financial need to work while also removing work-based structure and identity.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Tech companies might keep highly paid employees from retiring by convincing them that sudden wealth is dangerous and that continuing to work is therefore the safer choice.

preschool.title: The Fortune That Made Work Optional
preschool.lesson: Competitive AI pay and lucrative company sales can remove the financial need to work, but some newly wealthy people struggle when they also lose the routine, identity, and purpose their work provided.
paragraphs:
Top AI researchers command so much pay,
They could bank it, retire, and walk off that day.
To match rival offers, tech firms have to spend—
Then wonder why workers should work without end.

One joke: thirty million out by the Bay
Might buy two whole bedrooms, so don’t move away.
Another strange spur: researchers fear AI
Could end everyone—yet they still don’t say goodbye.

At Bloomberg Weekend, Tiffany Ap described
The strange aftershocks when big exits arrive.
That sparked a sly answer to tech’s hiring bind:
Make sudden wealth sound like a threat to peace of mind.

Anastasia Koroleva, a centimillionaire,
Asked ultra-rich guests what came after the fanfare.
Some called a $500 million company sale
A thing to “recover from,” dazed by its scale.
An exit means selling; the payday can close
Your need for a paycheck—but structure can go.

Psychologist Sherry Walling had seen
Founders meet every goal, yet feel far from serene.
She said Tony Hsieh’s death in 2020 helped people speak more openly about founders’ mental health.
Walling co-wrote Exit Strategy, a guide
